# i. Run PACS locally {.unnumbered}

## What a local PACS installation provides

Most users can work with PACS through the hosted website without installing
anything. A local installation is useful when you need:

- a private PACS instance for teaching or demonstrations;
- access when the hosted website is unavailable;
- a development environment for changing or testing PACS; or
- local control of the database and generated model results.

The recommended local installation uses Docker Compose. Docker builds and runs
the complete PACS stack as four coordinated services:

| Service | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **nginx** | Provides the single browser entry point at **http://localhost**. |
| **flask** | Serves the PACS website, authentication, database pages, and model routes. |
| **panel** | Serves the interactive model dashboards behind the Nginx proxy. |
| **db** | Runs MySQL and stores user accounts and site data in a persistent Docker volume. |

The PACS Docker image also installs MODFLOW 6. You do not need to install
Python, MySQL, Panel, or MODFLOW directly on the host computer when you use this
method.

## Install and verify the prerequisites

Install the following software before downloading PACS:

1. **Git**, used to download and update the source code.
2. **Docker with Docker Compose v2**.
   - On Windows and macOS, Docker Desktop includes Docker Compose.
   - On Linux, install Docker Engine and the Docker Compose plugin.
3. **A web browser**, such as Firefox, Chrome, Edge, or Safari.

The first build downloads container images, Python packages, and the official
MODFLOW 6 release. A stable internet connection is therefore required for the
first installation and for later updates that change the image.

Open PowerShell, Windows Terminal, Terminal, or another command shell and run:

~~~bash
git --version
docker --version
docker compose version
docker info
~~~

Each command should complete without an error. **docker info** confirms that the
Docker service is running, not only that the command-line program is installed.
If **docker info** cannot connect to the Docker daemon, start Docker Desktop or
the Docker service and try again.

::: {.callout-tip}
On Windows, wait until Docker Desktop reports that the engine is running before
continuing. Starting the application before Docker is ready is a common cause
of connection errors.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance=simple icon=false}

## Download the PACS source code

Choose a parent directory in which the new **cast** folder should be created.
Then clone the application repository:

~~~bash
git clone https://github.com/kamiz15/Groundwater-Contamination-Website.git cast
cd cast
~~~

The repository uses **final** as its default branch. A normal clone checks out
that branch automatically.

Confirm that the current directory contains at least these files:

~~~text
app.py
docker-compose.yml
Dockerfile
.env.example
.env.docker
~~~

Do not run **git clone** again if the **cast** directory already contains a
clone of the repository. Enter the existing directory with **cd cast**, check
that your work is saved, and use the update procedure in subsection vii
instead.

## Configure the local environment

PACS keeps secrets and machine-specific values in a file named **.env**. This
file is intentionally excluded from Git, which helps prevent passwords and
session keys from being committed to the repository.

***Create .env from the template***

Use the command for your shell.

PowerShell:

~~~powershell
Copy-Item .env.example .env
~~~

Command Prompt:

~~~bat
copy .env.example .env
~~~

macOS or Linux shell:

~~~bash
cp .env.example .env
~~~

Open **.env** in a text editor. For example, Windows users can run:

~~~powershell
notepad .env
~~~

***Set the four required values***

For a standard local Docker installation, replace the placeholder values for
these variables:

~~~dotenv
SECRET_KEY=replace_with_a_long_random_value
DB_USER=cast_user
DB_PASSWORD=replace_with_a_database_password
MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=replace_with_a_different_root_password
~~~

Do not copy the example values above unchanged. The purpose of each setting is:

| Variable | What it controls | Recommended local value |
|---|---|---|
| **SECRET_KEY** | Signs login sessions and security tokens. | A stable random value containing at least 32 random bytes. |
| **DB_USER** | Names the MySQL account used by PACS. | A simple name such as **cast_user**. |
| **DB_PASSWORD** | Protects the MySQL account used by PACS. | A long password that is different from the root password. |
| **MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD** | Protects the MySQL administrative account. | A second long password used only for database administration. |

The safest approach is to create the values with a password manager. If Python
is already installed, this command generates a 64-character hexadecimal value:

~~~bash
python -c print(__import__('secrets').token_hex(32))
~~~

If Python is not installed on the host, Docker can run the same generator:

~~~bash
docker run --rm python:3.11-slim python -c print(__import__('secrets').token_hex(32))
~~~

Run the generator three times. Use one result for **SECRET_KEY**, one for
**DB_PASSWORD**, and one for **MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD**. Hexadecimal output avoids
characters that can be interpreted specially by an environment file.

::: {.callout-important}
Keep the same **SECRET_KEY** after users have registered. Changing it signs out
existing sessions and invalidates security tokens.
:::

***Understand .env and .env.docker***

The two files have different roles:

- **.env** contains your private values. Docker Compose reads it for variable
  substitution. Do not commit or share this file.
- **.env.docker** contains tracked, non-secret settings for the container
  network. It tells PACS to use the **db** service, serve Panel through
  **/panel**, use plain HTTP cookies on localhost, and use the MODFLOW 6
  executable installed inside the image.

For the standard local Docker workflow, do not change **DB_HOST**,
**PANEL_PUBLIC_BASE**, **PANEL_ALLOW_ORIGINS**, or **MF6_EXE**. The correct
container values are already supplied by **.env.docker**.

The remaining entries copied from **.env.example** can normally keep their
defaults for a private local installation. In particular:

- **DB_NAME=cast_project** is the default database name.
- SMTP values may remain empty if email delivery is not configured.
- **DEMO_BYPASS_LOGIN** should remain **false** for normal use.
- **SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE** is already set to **false** in **.env.docker**
  because the local site uses **http://localhost**.

***Check the file before starting***

Make sure none of the four required values still contains a required-value
placeholder. Do not add spaces around the equals signs.

Validate the Compose configuration without printing the resolved secrets:

~~~bash
docker compose config --quiet
~~~

No output and an exit code of zero means that the Compose file can be resolved.
If Docker reports that a required variable is missing, reopen **.env**, correct
the named value, save the file, and run the validation command again.

You can also confirm that Git is ignoring the private file:

~~~bash
git status --short
~~~

The **.env** file should not appear in the output.

::: {.callout-warning}
The command **docker compose config** without **--quiet** prints the resolved
configuration and can include secret values. Do not copy that output into an
issue, chat message, screenshot, or public document.
:::

## Build and start PACS

From the repository root, run:

~~~bash
docker compose up --build -d
~~~

The options have the following meanings:

- **up** creates and starts the services.
- **--build** builds the PACS image from the current source code.
- **-d** leaves the services running in the background.

The first build can take several minutes. Docker downloads the base images,
installs the Python dependencies, downloads MODFLOW 6, creates the database
volume, and starts the four services. Later starts are usually faster because
Docker reuses downloaded layers.

Check the service state:

~~~bash
docker compose ps
~~~

The **nginx**, **flask**, **panel**, and **db** services should be running.
Services with health checks may briefly show **starting** before they show
**healthy**.

If a service does not become healthy, inspect recent logs:

~~~bash
docker compose logs --tail 100
~~~

To follow new log messages as they are written:

~~~bash
docker compose logs -f
~~~

Press **Ctrl+C** to stop following the logs. This does not stop the containers.

## Open and verify the local site

Open the following address in a browser:

<http://localhost>

Use **http**, not **https**, for the standard local configuration. Do not open
port 5000 or port 5007 when using Docker Compose. Nginx provides the intended
entry point on port 80 and routes model requests to the correct internal
service.

Complete this first-run check:

1. Confirm that the PACS home page loads.
2. Select **Sign Up** and register a local account.
3. Log in with the new account.
4. Open the site database.
5. Add one test site manually or upload a valid CSV file.
6. Open an analytical single-scenario page and confirm that the page loads.
7. Open a numerical page only after the other checks pass.
8. Run a small test scenario and confirm that a result is produced.

The MySQL database is created automatically during the first container start.
The Docker image already contains MODFLOW 6, so numerical pages do not require
a separate solver installation.

## Stop, restart, and update PACS

***Stop PACS without deleting data***

~~~bash
docker compose down
~~~

This stops and removes the containers and network. It keeps the named volumes
that contain MySQL data and queued numerical results.

***Start an existing installation***

~~~bash
docker compose up -d
~~~

Use **--build** as well when the application source, dependencies, or Dockerfile
has changed:

~~~bash
docker compose up --build -d
~~~

***Restart the running services***

~~~bash
docker compose restart
~~~

***Update PACS from GitHub***

First make sure any local code changes are committed or backed up. Then run:

~~~bash
git pull --ff-only
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose ps
~~~

The **.env** file and Docker data volumes are not replaced by **git pull**.

::: {.callout-warning}
Do not run **docker compose down -v** as part of a normal stop or update. The
**-v** option deletes the named volumes and permanently removes local accounts,
site data, and stored job data unless you have a separate backup.
:::

## Troubleshooting

***Docker cannot connect to the daemon***

Start Docker Desktop or the Docker service. Wait until it is ready, then run
**docker info** again.

***Port 80 is already in use***

Another web server may already be listening on port 80. Stop the conflicting
service, or change the host-side port in **docker-compose.yml** and open the new
port in the browser.

***A container is unhealthy or repeatedly restarts***

Identify the affected service:

~~~bash
docker compose ps
~~~

Then inspect only that service. Replace **flask** with **panel**, **db**, or
**nginx** when appropriate:

~~~bash
docker compose logs --tail 200 flask
~~~

***The database rejects the application password after .env was changed***

MySQL uses **DB_USER**, **DB_PASSWORD**, and **MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD** when the
database volume is created for the first time. Changing those values later does
not automatically change accounts inside an existing database. Restore the
previous values, or update the MySQL account deliberately before changing PACS
to use a new password. Do not delete the database volume unless losing its data
is acceptable.

***Login returns to the login page***

Confirm that the site was opened with **http://localhost** and that
**SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=false** remains in **.env.docker**. Secure cookies
require HTTPS and are not sent to the standard local HTTP address.

***Interactive model pages do not connect***

Use the Nginx address at **http://localhost**. The Compose configuration serves
Panel through the same-origin **/panel** path. Direct access to port 5007 is for
a different, non-Compose development setup.

***The first image build fails while downloading dependencies***

Confirm that Docker has internet access and retry:

~~~bash
docker compose up --build -d
~~~

Docker normally reuses completed layers, so the retry does not repeat every
successful step.
